item: Standing and interest: no one may litigate without standing (qualité) and a present or potential interest recognised by law (CPCA art. 13 para 1).

Who raises lack of standing: the judge raises lack of standing of the plaintiff or the defendant of his own motion (CPCA art. 13 para 2); check whether interest is also raised ex officio or only on a plea.
Authorisation: where a law requires an authorisation to sue (e.g. a guardian for a minor's property, a body that needs a deliberation), the judge raises its absence of his own motion (CPCA art. 13).

Form of the claim: the claim is brought by a written petition, signed and dated, filed at the court registry by the plaintiff, his agent or his lawyer, in as many copies as there are parties (CPCA art. 14).
Mandatory contents of the petition, on pain of formal inadmissibility (CPCA art. 15): the court seised.
Plaintiff's surname, first name and domicile (CPCA art. 15).
Defendant's surname, first name and domicile, or failing a known domicile his last known domicile (CPCA art. 15).
Legal person party: its nature, name, registered seat and the capacity of its legal or contractual representative (CPCA art. 15).
A summary statement of the facts, the requests and the means (grounds) relied on (CPCA art. 15).
Mention, where needed, of the supporting documents and evidence relied on (CPCA art. 15).

Sanction of a missing element: formal inadmissibility of the petition (non-acceptance in form), not nullity; check whether it can be cured by refiling and whether the court raises it of its own motion.

Registration: the registrar enters the petition in a register, numbers it, and notes the date of the first hearing; a delay of at least twenty days between service and the first hearing, extended to three months when the defendant resides abroad (CPCA art. 16).
Fees: registration of the petition requires payment of the judicial fees unless the law provides otherwise (legal aid) (CPCA art. 17 para 1).
Real-property petitions must be published at the land registry where the claim concerns rights subject to publication (CPCA art. 17) - import from land-registry-publication, do not restate.
Service: the petition is served on the defendant by a bailiff (commissaire de justice), at the plaintiff's initiative; a copy of the petition and the summons (CPCA art. 18-19).
Language: proceedings and acts must be in Arabic, and documents in a foreign language must be accompanied by an official translation, on pain of inadmissibility (CPCA art. 8).

Capacity and representation: lack of capacity of a party or lack of authority of a representative is a substantive nullity that the judge may raise of his own motion and that can be cured (CPCA art. 64-66).
Nullity for form of acts: no nullity without a text and proof of a grievance (CPCA art. 60).
Pleas of inadmissibility (lack of standing, lack of interest, limitation, forfeiture, res judicata) may be raised at any stage of the proceedings (CPCA art. 67-68).
Public-order inadmissibility (in particular for failure to respect time limits for remedies) must be raised by the judge of his own motion (CPCA art. 69).
Inadmissibility can be cured if its cause disappears before the judge rules (CPCA art. 67 or neighbouring article) - verify.

Lawyer: representation by a lawyer is not compulsory before the first-instance civil court (except where the law says so); compulsory before the administrative court (CPCA art. 826) and on appeal and cassation - verify, imports ordinary-court-exits for the administrative route.
Administrative petitions: signed by a lawyer, with a copy of the contested decision attached, on pain of inadmissibility (CPCA art. 815, 819) - boundary, not this module's civil petition.

Family section petitions: the family section is seised by petition under the general rules, with special provisions (CPCA art. 423-426) - verify what art. 426 adds (filing by the party in person, special documents).
Labour section: the petition must be accompanied by the record of non-conciliation (Law 90-04) - import labour-prelitigation.
Interest must be legitimate, personal and direct; a potential interest suffices only where the law allows (art. 13 'present or potential').
Standing of the public prosecutor as a main party in family matters (CPCA art. 3 bis of the Family Code / art. 260 CPCA) - boundary.
Legal person: standing is exercised through its legal representative; the state, wilaya and commune are represented by named officials (CPCA art. 828) - boundary to the administrative route.
Fees exemptions: legal aid (Ordinance 71-57 as amended) and statutory exemptions (workers in labour claims under Law 90-04 art. ?) - check whether in the store.
Documents to attach: copies of the supporting documents listed in the petition; communication of documents to the opponent (CPCA art. 21-23).
Amendment of requests: incidental and additional requests after filing (CPCA art. 25) - boundary.
Amendments: CPCA Law 08-09 (2008) amended by Law 22-13 (2022), which notably created the specialised commercial courts and touched art. 32 and following; check whether art. 13-17 were touched.

What looks like a defect in the petition and is not: territorial incompetence (imported territorial-jurisdiction), the wrong section (imported court-sections), lack of formal notice (imported formal-notice) - each has its own sanction.

The 22 Legal Review questions: each mandatory field of the form (court, parties, legal person representative, facts, requests, means, documents, signature, date, place) must map to an article and a sanction.
Does the plaintiff have capacity to sue (full civil capacity, or a legal representative)?
Does the plaintiff have standing (a personal right or legal position at stake)?
Does the plaintiff have a legitimate interest, existing or at least potential?
Does the court raise lack of standing or of interest of its own motion, or only on a party's objection?
Is the petition in writing, in Arabic, signed by the plaintiff or his lawyer, and dated?
Is the petition filed at the court registry with enough copies for the defendants?
Does the petition name the court that will hear it?
Does the petition give the plaintiff's surname, first name and domicile?
Does the petition give the defendant's surname, first name and domicile, or his last known domicile?
For a legal person, does the petition give its nature, name, registered seat and its representative?
Does the petition give a brief statement of the facts?
Does the petition state the claims (what is asked of the court) and the grounds relied on?
Does the petition list the documents and evidence attached to it?
Are the supporting documents attached in the right number of copies?
What is the consequence if a mandatory element is missing: inadmissibility, a request to regularise, or nothing?
Can the defect be cured later, and until when?
Is the petition registered by the registry only after the judicial fees are paid?
What fee is due at filing, and who is exempt (legal aid, the State, certain matters)?
What happens if the fee is not paid: refusal to register, a time to pay, or inadmissibility?
Does the petition have to state the date of the first hearing and the summons period?
Is a lawyer mandatory before this court or this kind of claim?
Must the petition cite the legal text relied on?
Must the petition state the amount claimed when it is a money claim?
Does a joinder of several claims or several defendants change the petition's form?
Does the family-matters section require anything more in the petition (the conciliation, the public prosecutor)?
Is a petition lodged by a person without standing void or only inadmissible?
Does the interest have to exist at filing, or may it arise later?
Can a third party intervene or be called in, and how must that request be made?
Which prior steps must be shown with the petition (notice, conciliation record, publication)?
Does the petition interrupt a limitation period by being filed, and from what date?
